Old age
With aging, there is a decline in total body water, in both the extracellular and intracellular ﬂuid volume. There is also decreased
ﬂuid intake related to decreased thirst due to a higher osmotic operating point (the point at which the thirst sensation is triggered).
Aging is also associated with a reduced glomerular ﬁltration rate, increased proximal tubular renal absorption and a decline in
maximal tubular ﬂuid concentrating ability (Thomas et al., 2008).
The normal nocturnal rise that occurs with AVP is blunted with aging resulting in nocturia. These physiological changes that
occur with aging place older persons at major risk for dehydration.
Certain behavioral factors may also inﬂuence drinking patterns in older adults who may wish to avoid the physical difﬁculty
associated with trips to the bathroom. Dehydration also alters the effective dosage of medications through plasma volume changes,
leading to further medical complications in the elderly. Dehydration in the elderly often accompanies or results from clinical condi-
tions and/or medications.
People who work or exercise outside
When the weather is hot and humid, risk of dehydration and heat illness increases. When the air is humid, sweat can’t evaporate and
cool as quickly as it normally does, and this can lead to an increased body temperature and the need for more ﬂuids.
